verses.context: Paul opens the longest greeting in any of his letters. In Greek, verses 1-7 are a single sentence, and before he names his readers he has packed into it a summary of the gospel itself. Here he gives three descriptions of himself, each defining him by someone else's act: he belongs to Christ, he was called, and he was set apart.
verses.grammar: Doulos Christou Iēsou is ‘slave of Christ Jesus’, a possessive genitive; the Old Testament gives the phrase dignity by calling Moses, Joshua, and David servants of the LORD, but the Greek word never loses its sense of ownership. Klētos apostolos uses a verbal adjective, ‘a called apostle’: apostle by summons, not by self-appointment (compare Galatians 1:1). Aphōrismenos is a perfect passive participle, ‘having been set apart’, describing a past act with a lasting result, and the passive leaves God as the unnamed actor. Paul uses the same verb in Galatians 1:15 for God setting him apart from his mother's womb, language that echoes the call of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:5) and of the servant in Isaiah 49:1. The phrase euangelion theou, ‘the gospel of God’, is a genitive of source: the good news comes from God, and verse 3 will say what it is about.
verses.text: Printed editions differ on the order of the names. The Nestle-Aland and SBL editions print ‘Christ Jesus’, while Westcott and Hort, the Tyndale House edition, the Textus Receptus, and the Byzantine text print ‘Jesus Christ’. The manuscripts divide, the two orders are equally Pauline, and the meaning is unaffected.

theology.note: Paul's authority rests on a commission, not on personal gifts or standing. The verse defines the apostle as one sent and set apart by God for a message he did not invent, which is why the letter can speak with authority to a church Paul did not found.

verses.context: Before saying what the gospel is, Paul says where it came from: it is not a new religion but the fulfillment of what God promised through Israel's prophets. The claim anticipates the whole argument of the letter, which quotes the Old Testament more than fifty times and returns to this point at 3:21 and in the closing doxology (16:25-26).
verses.grammar: Proepēngeilato is an aorist middle verb compounded with pro-, ‘promised beforehand’. The prefix does the theological work: the promise preceded the fulfillment, so the gospel cannot be judged a novelty. The phrase en graphais hagiais, ‘in holy Scriptures’, has no article, an unusual expression in Paul that stresses the character of the writings (holy ones) rather than pointing to a collection by name.

theology.note: The gospel is presented as promise kept. Paul reads the prophets as speaking ahead of time of God's Son, which is how the apostles consistently read Israel's Scriptures (Luke 24:27, Acts 26:22-23).
Paul assumes a body of writings his Gentile and Jewish readers both recognize as holy and authoritative. The New Testament's first claim about the Old is that it belongs to the gospel.

verses.context: The gospel is about a person, God's Son, described in two balanced clauses: descended from David in the sphere of the flesh, and declared Son of God in power in the sphere of the Spirit by resurrection. The rhythm and the unusual vocabulary have led most scholars to think Paul is quoting or adapting an early Jewish-Christian confession that he expects the Roman church to recognize, a way of establishing common ground with readers who had never met him.
verses.grammar: The two participles are set in parallel: genomenou, ‘having come to be’, from the seed of David, and horisthentos, from horizō, ‘appointed’ or ‘designated’ (the same verb is used of Christ appointed judge in Acts 10:42 and 17:31). The BSB's ‘declared’ guards against reading the verse as though Jesus became Son at the resurrection; the phrase en dynamei, ‘in power’, probably goes with ‘Son of God’, so that the one who was already Son (verse 3 calls him ‘His Son’ before either clause) was installed as Son-of-God-in-power. That is the reading of C. E. B. Cranfield (ICC, 1975) and most commentators. The contrast kata sarka and kata pneuma hagiōsynēs, ‘according to flesh’ and ‘according to a Spirit of holiness’, was read by many church fathers as Christ's human and divine natures; many modern interpreters, among them James Dunn, read it instead as two eras, the Son's earthly life and his risen life in the power of the Spirit. The phrase ‘Spirit of holiness’ is Semitic in shape and appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Ex anastaseōs nekrōn is literally ‘from a resurrection of dead people’, not ‘from the dead’: Jesus' rising is the first instance of the general resurrection of the last day.

ot.note: God's promise to David stands behind both clauses. In Hebrew, God says he will raise up (vahaqimoti) David's offspring (zar'akha) after him, establish his kingdom, and be a father to him, and he will be a son to God. The Septuagint renders it with anastēsō to sperma sou, ‘I will raise up your seed’, using the verb whose noun, anastasis, Paul uses for resurrection. Paul's wording picks up both words: the Son comes ek spermatos Dauid, from David's seed, and is designated Son ex anastaseōs, by resurrection. In its original setting the promise concerned David's dynasty, beginning with Solomon; by Paul's day it was read of a coming Davidic king, and Paul announces that God has raised him up in a fuller sense than Nathan's hearers could have known. Psalm 2:7, where God addresses the king as his son on the day of his installation, is quoted of the resurrection in Acts 13:33 and is probably in the background too.

verses.history: The pairing of 2 Samuel 7 and Psalm 2 was not a Christian invention. The Qumran text known as 4QFlorilegium (4Q174), copied in the first century BC, quotes God's promise to David in 2 Samuel 7:11-14 and interprets the one who will be God's son as the Branch of David who will arise in the last days, then moves on to Psalm 2. Paul's confession shares that Jewish messianic reading and makes one decisive claim: the promised son of David has been identified, and the event that identifies him is his resurrection.

theology.note: Jesus is David's heir according to the flesh. Paul's gospel begins with Israel's king, not with a general religious idea, and the royal promise to David is the frame in which the Gentile mission of verse 5 makes sense.

The resurrection is the public act by which God installs his Son in power. It is also, by Paul's phrasing, the beginning of the resurrection of the dead: what happened to Jesus is the first fruits of what will happen to his people (1 Corinthians 15:20).

The Son is called God's Son before the clause about David, so the verse assumes his sonship precedes his human birth. He ‘came to be’ from David's line; he did not begin to be. Philippians 2:6-8 and Galatians 4:4 draw the same line.

verses.context: From the risen Lord Paul received his commission, and its goal is named: the obedience of faith among all the nations. Verse 6 then brings the Roman believers inside the scope of that mission, which is why Paul has standing to write to them. The phrase about the obedience of faith returns at the letter's close (16:26), framing the whole.
verses.grammar: Charin kai apostolēn, ‘grace and apostleship’, is probably a hendiadys, two nouns naming one thing: the grace of being an apostle (compare 12:3 and 15:15, where Paul speaks of the grace given him). The phrase hypakoēn pisteōs, ‘obedience of faith’, has a genitive that can be read three ways: obedience that consists in faith (an appositional genitive), obedience that springs from faith (a genitive of source, the BSB's ‘that comes from faith’), or faithful obedience. Don Garlington's study (The Obedience of Faith, 1991) argued that Paul chose the phrase for its breadth, so that believing and obeying are not separated. In verse 6, klētoi Iēsou Christou is best taken as possessive, ‘called ones belonging to Jesus Christ’, since in Paul it is God the Father who calls (8:30). Ethnesin can mean nations or Gentiles; here it covers the non-Jewish world to which Paul was sent.

theology.note: The purpose of Paul's apostleship is the faith-obedience of every nation, for the sake of Christ's name. Mission in Romans is not recruitment to a group but the extension of Christ's rightful lordship over the peoples promised to Abraham (4:17-18).

By joining obedience and faith in one phrase, Paul shows that the faith he preaches is not bare assent. Faith submits to the one it trusts, which is why the letter can teach justification by faith apart from works and still end in chapters 12-15 with a whole life reshaped.

verses.context: The address and greeting finally arrive. The readers are named by three things God has done for them: they are beloved by God, called, and holy. The greeting, grace and peace, is Paul's standard Christian adaptation of the conventional Greek and Jewish letter openings.
verses.grammar: Klētois hagiois is literally ‘called saints’; the BSB supplies ‘to be’, but the Greek has no verb, and the sense is that they are saints by God's calling, not by moral achievement. The phrase recalls the Greek Old Testament's klētē hagia, ‘holy convocation’, used for Israel's sacred assemblies (Leviticus 23:3), so the Gentile believers in Rome are addressed with Israel's own vocabulary. In the blessing, God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ stand together after a single preposition, apo, as the one source of grace and peace. Paul does this in every letter opening without comment, which shows how early and how naturally the first Christians placed Jesus alongside God as the giver of divine gifts.
verses.text: A few witnesses lack the words ‘in Rome’. The ninth-century Greek-Latin Codex Boernerianus reads ‘to all who are in the love of God’ here and leaves out ‘in Rome’ in verse 15 as well, and some other traces of the omission survive. Harry Gamble (The Textual History of the Letter to the Romans, 1977) connected this with an early shortened form of Romans that circulated without its specifically Roman details, as a general letter to the churches. The overwhelming manuscript evidence has ‘in Rome’, and every modern edition prints it.

theology.note: The church is defined first by God's love and call, and holiness is given before it is achieved. Paul will spend chapters 6 and 12-15 on how saints live, but here he establishes that they are saints.

Grace and peace come jointly from the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The verse does not state a doctrine of the Trinity, but it shows the pattern of worship and prayer out of which the church later confessed the Son as one in being with the Father (compare Larry Hurtado, Lord Jesus Christ, 2003, on early devotion to Jesus).

verses.context: The thanksgiving section begins, as in most of Paul's letters. He thanks God that the Romans' faith is known everywhere, calls God as witness to his constant prayer for them, and states the prayer's content: that he may at last reach them. These verses establish warmth with a church that did not know him, and verse 10 leads into the explanation of why he has not come.
verses.grammar: Prōton men, ‘first’, is never followed by a ‘second’; Paul begins a list and is carried off by the content, a common feature of his dictated style. Martys gar mou estin ho theos, ‘God is my witness’, is an oath formula, used when Paul's sincerity could be doubted (2 Corinthians 1:23, Philippians 1:8, 1 Thessalonians 2:5). The verb latreuō, ‘I serve’, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for priestly and cultic worship, so Paul describes his preaching as worship offered ‘in my spirit’, the thought he develops in 12:1 and 15:16, where he calls himself a priestly minister of the gospel to the Gentiles. In verse 10, ei pōs ēdē pote, ‘if somehow now at last’, piles up four small particles that express eager but uncertain hope. The verb euodōthēsomai (future passive) means ‘I will be granted success’, with God's will as the governing condition.
verses.history: The Roman historian Suetonius (Claudius 25.4) reports that Claudius expelled Jews from Rome because of disturbances ‘at the instigation of Chrestus’, which most historians take as a garbled reference to disputes over Christ in the synagogues. Acts 18:2 connects Priscilla and Aquila's arrival in Corinth with that expulsion. By the time Paul writes, about AD 57, the believers in Rome were known in the churches he had planted in the East, and Priscilla and Aquila were back in the city (16:3-5). A decade later, Tacitus (Annals 15.44) would describe the Christians of Rome as numerous enough for Nero to blame them for the fire of AD 64.

theology.note: Paul's prayer is ceaseless, specific, and submitted to God's will. His thanks are offered ‘through Jesus Christ’: even gratitude reaches God through the mediator.

verses.context: Paul explains the longing behind the prayer: he wants to give the Romans something that will strengthen them. Then, as if hearing how that might sound to a church he did not found, he restates it as mutual encouragement. The apostle expects to receive as well as give.
verses.grammar: Charisma pneumatikon, ‘spiritual gift’, is qualified by the indefinite ti, ‘some’, so Paul does not specify a particular gift of the kind listed in 12:6-8; he may mean the strengthening that the letter itself begins to provide. Stērichthēnai is an aorist passive infinitive, ‘to be strengthened’, with God as the implied agent (compare 16:25, where God is ‘able to strengthen you’). Verse 12 opens with touto de estin, ‘that is’, a self-correction. The compound infinitive symparaklēthēnai, ‘to be encouraged together’, occurs only here in the New Testament, and the phrase ‘each other's faith, both yours and mine’ puts the apostle and the congregation on the same level.

theology.note: A spiritual gift is given for others' strengthening, not for the giver's status. Even an apostle's gift works both ways in the church, a principle Paul develops in 12:3-8.
Faith is built up in company. Paul does not picture himself as a supplier and the Romans as consumers; believers strengthen one another's faith by sharing it.

verses.context: Paul explains that his absence has not been neglect: he has often planned to come and has been prevented. His motive is a harvest among them like the one he has seen elsewhere, and behind that motive is a debt he owes to every kind of person. Verse 15 draws the conclusion, and verse 16 will give its ground.
verses.grammar: Ou thelō de hymas agnoein, ‘I do not want you to be unaware’, is a formula Paul uses to introduce important information (11:25, 1 Corinthians 10:1, 12:1, 2 Corinthians 1:8, 1 Thessalonians 4:13). Ekōlythēn, ‘I was hindered’, is passive and does not name the hindrance; 15:19-23 later explains it as the unfinished work in the eastern provinces. Opheiletēs eimi, ‘I am a debtor’, makes Paul's obligation not to those who gave him something but to those for whom he was given something: the gospel entrusted to him is owed to them. Verse 15 is compressed Greek, houtōs to kat' eme prothymon, literally ‘so, as far as it lies with me, the eagerness’. The infinitive euangelisasthai, ‘to proclaim the gospel’, is addressed to people who already believe, which shows that for Paul the gospel is not only the entry point but the continuing substance of the Christian life, as the letter that follows demonstrates.
verses.history: Paul's plan to see Rome is recorded in Acts 19:21, when he was in Ephesus, and in Romans 15:23-29 he explains the route: first to Jerusalem with the collection from the Gentile churches of Macedonia and Achaia, then to Rome, then on to Spain. He did reach Rome, about three years later, but as a prisoner (Acts 28:14-16). Whether he ever reached Spain is uncertain; 1 Clement 5.7, written from Rome near the end of the first century, says he reached the limit of the West, which some read as Spain.

theology.note: The pairs of verse 14 cover every cultural and educational divide Paul's world recognized. The gospel is owed to all of them equally, and the apostle cannot choose his hearers by their sophistication.

verses.context: Verses 16-17 state the theme of the whole letter, and they are joined to what precedes by a chain of ‘for’ clauses. Paul is eager to preach in Rome (verse 15) because he is not ashamed of the gospel (verse 16a), because it is God's power for salvation (verse 16b), because in it God's righteousness is revealed (verse 17). The word ‘everyone’ and the phrase about Jew and Greek announce the question Paul will keep returning to through chapter 11.
verses.grammar: Ou epaischynomai, ‘I am not ashamed’, is understatement that implies its opposite, and it is not merely emotional. In the Psalms and prophets, being put to shame means being exposed as having trusted in something that failed, and Paul later quotes Isaiah 28:16, that whoever believes in him will not be put to shame (9:33, 10:11). The gospel is dynamis theou, God's power, not advice about God. Panti tō pisteuonti is a present participle, ‘everyone who believes’, marking the recipients by their continuing trust. Ioudaiō te prōton kai Hellēni binds Jew and Greek with te kai, ‘both and’, while prōton, ‘first’, gives Israel a real priority in the order of God's promises (compare 3:1-2 and chapters 9-11) without giving it a different gospel.
verses.history: The shame Paul refuses was real. Crucifixion was the Roman death for slaves and rebels, and Cicero, defending Gaius Rabirius in 63 BC (For Rabirius 16), said the very word for cross should be kept far from a Roman citizen's thoughts, eyes, and ears. A message whose center was a crucified Jew was, in Paul's words to Corinth, foolishness to Greeks and a stumbling block to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23). To announce it in the capital of the empire that crucified him was to invite contempt.
verses.text: The Textus Receptus and Byzantine manuscripts read ‘the gospel of Christ’, which is why the King James Version has that phrase. The earliest manuscripts have simply ‘the gospel’, and the words ‘of Christ’ are best explained as a scribal filling out of the phrase.

theology.note: Salvation is God's own power at work, received by believing. Because the one condition is faith, the offer is universal, and because the gospel is God's power, no hearer is beyond it.
The gospel is for the Jew first. Paul does not treat Israel's priority as cancelled by the Gentile mission; it is the order in which God keeps his promises, and chapters 9-11 are his defense of it.

verses.context: The theme's second half gives the reason the gospel is power: in it God's righteousness is being revealed, on the basis of faith and for faith, as Habakkuk had said. The next verse begins with ‘for’ and sets a second revelation beside this one, the revelation of God's wrath, which Paul must explain first (1:18-3:20) before he returns to God's righteousness in 3:21 with the same words.
verses.grammar: The phrase dikaiosynē theou, ‘righteousness of God’, is the hinge of the letter, and the genitive theou can be read three ways. As a subjective or possessive genitive it names God's own righteousness, either his justice or his saving activity; Ernst Käsemann's 1961 essay on the righteousness of God in Paul read it as God's saving power reclaiming the world, a gift that carries the lordship of the giver within it. As a genitive of source it names the right standing that comes from God and is given to believers, which is how Paul words it in Philippians 3:9 (tēn ek theou dikaiosynēn, ‘the righteousness from God’); Rudolf Bultmann and C. E. B. Cranfield took this view. As an objective genitive it is the righteousness that counts before God, the sense of Luther's German Bible, which renders it ‘the righteousness that is valid before God’. Two features of the context pull in different directions: the parallel with ‘the wrath of God’ in verse 18 suggests God's own action, while 3:22 and 5:17 speak of righteousness received as a gift. Many commentators, among them Douglas Moo, conclude that Paul means God's act of putting people right with himself, an act that results in a status. The verb apokalyptetai is present: the righteousness is being revealed now, wherever the gospel is proclaimed (‘in it’).

ot.note: The Hebrew reads vetsaddiq be'emunato yichyeh, ‘the righteous by his faithfulness will live’, where ‘his’ most naturally means the righteous person's steady trust. Habakkuk had complained that God was raising up Babylon against Judah; the answer was a vision to be written down and waited for, and the one who is righteous will live by holding faithfully to it while the proud collapse. The Septuagint reads ho de dikaios ek pisteōs mou zēsetai, ‘the righteous will live by my faithfulness’, that is, God's; some manuscripts of it put the pronoun with ‘righteous’ instead (‘my righteous one will live by faith’), the order Hebrews 10:38 follows. Paul drops the pronoun altogether, which leaves the verse open to cover both the faithfulness of God and the faith of the one who trusts him. He quotes it again in Galatians 3:11. The syntax is debated: ek pisteōs may go with ‘will live’ (most English versions) or with ‘the righteous’, as Anders Nygren argued and the RSV rendered it, ‘he who through faith is righteous shall live’. On Nygren's reading, Romans 1-4 explains the first half (righteous by faith) and 5-8 the second (shall live). Richard Hays and Douglas Campbell have argued that Paul reads ‘the righteous one’ messianically, of Christ; most interpreters hold that he means any believer.

verses.history: Habakkuk 2:4 was important to Jews before Paul and after him. The Qumran commentary on Habakkuk (1QpHab 8:1-3) applies it to those in the house of Judah who keep the law, whom God will deliver because of their toil and their faith in the Teacher of Righteousness. The Babylonian Talmud (Makkot 23b-24a) records Rabbi Simlai's teaching that the 613 commandments were summarized by successive prophets until Habakkuk based them all on one, this verse. Martin Luther, in the preface to the 1545 edition of his Latin works, described his breakthrough as the realization that the righteousness of God in this verse is the righteousness by which God, in mercy, justifies the believer.
verses.text: ‘From faith to faith’ (ek pisteōs eis pistin) is translated very differently in English Bibles: ‘from faith for faith’ (ESV), ‘by faith from first to last’ (NIV), and ‘by faith from start to finish’ (BSB). Readings include from God's faithfulness to human faith (James Dunn), from the preacher's faith to the hearer's, from growing faith to more faith, and simply ‘by faith through and through’. The last is supported by similar idioms, ‘from death to death’ in 2 Corinthians 2:16 and the Septuagint's ‘from strength to strength’ in Psalm 84:7, where the repetition intensifies rather than marks two stages.

theology.note: This verse announces the doctrine the letter explains. Interpreters differ on its center. The Reformation tradition reads God's righteousness as the right standing God gives the sinner by faith. The New Perspective, associated with James Dunn (Romans 1-8, 1988) and N. T. Wright (What Saint Paul Really Said, 1997), reads it chiefly as God's faithfulness to his covenant promises, by which he creates one family of Jews and Gentiles. Critics such as Stephen Westerholm (Perspectives Old and New on Paul, 2004), Mark Seifrid, and Charles Lee Irons (The Righteousness of God, 2015) have argued that the Hebrew and Greek righteousness words concern God's justice and right order rather than covenant faithfulness as such. Many hold that God's saving action and the gift it bestows belong together in the phrase.

The righteousness God reveals is received on the basis of faith and for faith. Faith here is not a contribution that earns; it is the posture of the one who lives by God's faithfulness, as Habakkuk's righteous man waited on God's vision.

verses.context: The ‘for’ that opens this verse explains why the gospel's revelation of righteousness is needed: God's wrath is also being revealed, against all human godlessness. This begins the first main section of the letter (1:18-3:20), the indictment. The two ‘revealed’ verbs (verses 17 and 18) stand side by side, and the rest of the letter shows how the one answers the other.
verses.grammar: Apokalyptetai, ‘is being revealed’, repeats the verb of verse 17 in the same present tense, so the wrath is not only future (2:5 speaks of a coming day of wrath) but already at work; verses 24-28 will show how. Asebeia and adikia, ‘godlessness and wickedness’, name sin against God and sin against others, though the second may summarize the first. The participle katechontōn can mean ‘holding’ or ‘holding down’. The King James Version's ‘who hold the truth in unrighteousness’ suggests people who possess the truth but live unrighteously; nearly all modern versions read ‘suppress’, which fits the argument of verses 19-21 that people knew and refused.

theology.note: God's wrath is his settled, personal opposition to evil, revealed now as well as at the last day. C. H. Dodd (Moffatt commentary, 1932) described it as an impersonal process of cause and effect in a moral universe; Leon Morris (The Apostolic Preaching of the Cross, 1955) replied that in Scripture wrath is God's own response, though never capricious. The verse's parallel with God's righteousness supports the second: both are God's acts.
The root of human wrongdoing is identified as the suppression of truth. Sin begins not in ignorance but in resistance to what is known.

verses.context: Paul explains why the suppression of verse 18 is culpable: God has made himself known through what he made. Since creation, his eternal power and divinity have been visible to the mind, and so no one can plead ignorance. The argument is about accountability, not about the route to salvation.
verses.grammar: Dioti, ‘because’, grounds verse 18. To gnōston tou theou can mean ‘what is known about God’ or ‘what can be known about God’; either way Paul claims real, not merely possible, knowledge, since he adds that God himself made it plain (ephanerōsen, aorist). Verse 20 is built on a deliberate paradox: ta aorata, ‘the invisible things’, kathoratai, ‘are clearly seen’, with nooumena, ‘being understood’, showing that the seeing is perception by the mind through tois poiēmasin, ‘the things made’. Theiotēs, ‘divinity’ or ‘divine nature’, occurs only here in the New Testament and names God's divine character in general, not the specific word theotēs, ‘deity’, of Colossians 2:9. The closing phrase eis to einai autous anapologētous can express purpose (so that they would be without excuse) or result (with the result that they are); most grammarians take it as result.
verses.history: The argument from the order of the world to a divine maker was familiar to Paul's Greek readers. Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods (book 2, 45 BC) gives the Stoic version at length through the speaker Balbus, and Hellenistic Jewish writers used the same reasoning against idolatry. Paul's own sermons in Acts appeal to creation in speaking to Gentiles (Acts 14:15-17 at Lystra, 17:24-28 at Athens). What distinguishes Romans is the conclusion drawn: the knowledge was real, and it was refused.

theology.note: These verses are the classic text for what theologians call general revelation. The First Vatican Council (Dei Filius, 1870) cited verse 20 in teaching that God can be known with certainty by the natural light of reason. John Calvin (Institutes 1.3-5) spoke of an innate sense of the divine and of creation as a theater of God's glory, but stressed that sin blinds people to it. In 1934 Karl Barth, in his reply Nein to Emil Brunner, rejected any natural theology as a point of contact for the gospel. Paul's own conclusion is limited and pointed: creation's witness leaves people accountable, not saved.
The created world is not neutral. By its existence and order it testifies to its Maker, so that the refusal to honor God is a refusal of what creation itself declares (Psalm 19:1-4).

verses.context: Paul now narrates the refusal. Humanity knew God and did not give him glory or thanks; the result was futile thinking, darkened hearts, and a wisdom that turned into folly. The narrative is told in past tenses as a single story of the human race, and it leads directly into the exchange of verse 23.
verses.grammar: Gnontes, an aorist participle, is concessive: ‘although they knew God’. The failure is named precisely: they did not glorify him as God (edoxasan) or give thanks (ēucharistēsan), so the root sin is a refusal of worship and gratitude, not first a moral lapse. The two passive verbs that follow, emataiōthēsan, ‘they were made futile’, and eskotisthē, ‘was darkened’, describe what happened to them as a consequence. Mataioō belongs to the Septuagint's vocabulary for idolatry: in Jeremiah 2:5 Israel's fathers went after worthless things and became worthless, using the same verb. Phaskontes (present participle), ‘claiming’, sets pretension against reality, and emōranthēsan, ‘they became fools’, echoes Jeremiah's description of idol-makers made foolish by their knowledge (Jeremiah 10:14).

theology.note: Ingratitude and the refusal of worship come before the making of images. Idolatry, in Paul's account, begins in the heart that will not give thanks, and its first fruit is distorted thinking.

Sin damages the mind. The darkening is not only moral but intellectual: people who reject the truth about God lose the ability to think truly about the world, which Paul answers in 12:2 with the renewing of the mind.

verses.context: The central act of the indictment is an exchange: the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal creatures. The verbs of exchange will return in verses 25 and 26, each time followed by God's handing over, so this verse sets the pattern of the whole passage.
verses.grammar: Ēllaxan, ‘they exchanged’, takes its object with en, ‘for’ or ‘into’, a construction taken over from the Greek Old Testament. The phrase en homoiōmati eikonos, ‘in a likeness of an image’, doubles its terms, putting two steps of distance between the worshiper and the reality: not even the creature, but the image of its likeness. The adjectives aphthartou, ‘immortal’, and phthartou, ‘mortal’, differ by a single letter in Greek, a play that sharpens the absurdity of the trade. The sequence of man, birds, four-footed animals, and creeping things recalls the creatures of Genesis 1:20-26 and the prohibited images of Deuteronomy 4:16-18. Morna Hooker's article on Adam in Romans 1 (New Testament Studies, 1960) argued that Paul tells humanity's idolatry in language that echoes Adam's fall, a reading that has become widely held.

ot.note: The psalm recalls the golden calf at Sinai. The Hebrew says Israel exchanged (vayyamiru) their glory, that is, God, for the image (betavnit) of an ox that eats grass. The Septuagint (Psalm 105:20 in its numbering) renders it kai ēllaxanto tēn doxan autōn en homoiōmati moschou, using the same verb, the same noun for glory, and the same phrase ‘in a likeness’ that Paul uses. Jeremiah 2:11 makes the same charge: God's people changed their glory for what does not profit. By borrowing words written about Israel's own idolatry to describe the Gentile world, Paul prepares the turn of chapter 2, where the Jewish reader is shown to stand inside the same indictment.

theology.note: God's glory is his own revealed majesty, and human beings were made to reflect it. Exchanging it for images is the reverse of the human vocation, which is why Paul later says all have sinned and lack God's glory (3:23) and that believers are being restored to it (8:29-30).
Humanity, made in God's image, made images of creatures and worshiped them. The echo of Genesis 1 suggests that idolatry distorts the very thing that makes human beings human.

verses.context: The first of three handings over. Because (dio, ‘therefore’) people exchanged God's glory, God gave them over to the desires they already had, and the result was the degrading of their own bodies. Verse 25 restates the cause in stronger terms, the truth exchanged for the lie, and breaks off in a blessing of the Creator, as a devout Jew would on naming God.
verses.grammar: Paredōken, ‘he handed over’, is the verb for delivering someone into custody or to another's power; Stephen uses it in Acts 7:42 of God giving Israel over to worship the host of heaven. God's judgment here consists in letting the chosen course run: en tais epithymiais, ‘in the desires’, shows they were already in them. The infinitive atimazesthai, ‘to be dishonored’, expresses the result. In verse 25, hoitines is a qualitative relative (‘people who’) that gives the reason. Tō pseudei has the article, ‘the lie’, probably the idol itself (compare Isaiah 44:20). The phrase para ton ktisanta can mean ‘rather than the Creator’ or ‘beyond, in preference to the Creator’; either way the creature displaces God. Eulogētos eis tous aiōnas, amēn, ‘blessed forever, amen’, is the form of the Jewish benediction (berakhah).

theology.note: Idolatry is worship and service given to what is made. Paul pairs the two verbs, reverence and service, because idols claim both the heart and the life, and whatever is served in place of God eventually degrades the one who serves it.
God's present wrath takes the form of giving people what they insist on. The judgment is fitting: those who dishonored God find themselves dishonoring their own bodies.

verses.context: The second handing over. Paul's example of dishonorable passions is same-sex relations among women and men, described as exchanging the natural for the unnatural. The word ‘exchanged’ in verse 26 ties this to verses 23 and 25: in Paul's argument the disorder in desire mirrors the prior disorder in worship. The debates over these verses are summarized in the chapter note; the notes here concern their wording and setting.
verses.grammar: Dia touto, ‘for this reason’, links the handing over to the exchange of verse 25. Paul uses thēleiai and arsenes, the words for ‘female’ and ‘male’, rather than the ordinary words for women and men; they are the terms of Genesis 1:27 in the Septuagint (arsen kai thēly), which many interpreters take as a signal that Paul is thinking of the created order. Physikēn chrēsin, ‘natural use’, uses chrēsis, a common Greek term for sexual relations, and para physin means ‘contrary to nature’. The verb exekauthēsan, ‘they were inflamed’, is passive, and orexis, ‘desire’, occurs only here in the New Testament. The ‘due penalty for their error’ (antimisthian... tēs planēs) most likely refers to the error of idolatry: the disorder itself is the recompense, received ‘in themselves’.
verses.history: The phrase ‘contrary to nature’ (para physin) had a history. Plato's Laws (636c) calls same-sex pleasure between males and between females contrary to nature, and the Jewish writers Philo and Josephus used the same contrast; Josephus says the law recognizes only intercourse according to nature, with a wife (Against Apion 2.199). Paul also uses physis elsewhere: of custom about hair length (1 Corinthians 11:14) and of God grafting Gentiles into Israel's olive tree contrary to nature (Romans 11:24). Readers of verse 26 differ on its reference. Most since John Chrysostom (Homilies on Romans 4) have read it of relations between women, a reading Bernadette Brooten (Love Between Women, 1996) supports from ancient sources; some early and modern readers have taken it of unnatural acts between men and women.

theology.note: Paul presents disordered desire as a symptom of a deeper disorder, the refusal to honor the Creator. His argument concerns what humanity as a whole has become, not a ranking of sinners, and the next chapter will insist that the one who judges stands under the same verdict.

The appeal to what is natural grounds Paul's sexual ethic in creation rather than in custom alone, in the traditional reading, while revisionist readers argue that his idea of nature is shaped by ancient assumptions. Churches remain divided on how the verses apply today, as the chapter note sets out.

verses.context: The third handing over reaches the mind itself. Because people did not think God worth acknowledging, God gave them over to a mind that fails every test, and the result is conduct that is unfitting. The verse introduces the vice list that follows.
verses.grammar: The verse turns on a wordplay: ouk edokimasan, ‘they did not approve’, that is, they tested God and found him not worth keeping in their knowledge, so God gave them over to an adokimon noun, a ‘disapproved’ or ‘unqualified’ mind, one that fails the test. The punishment answers the sin in the same vocabulary. Ta mē kathēkonta, ‘what is not fitting’, uses a Stoic technical term for appropriate duties (kathēkonta), so Paul describes the result in terms his philosophically educated readers would recognize. Epignōsis, ‘knowledge’ or ‘acknowledgment’, implies recognition and response, not bare information.

theology.note: God's judgment corresponds to the offense. Those who judged God unworthy of acknowledgment are given a mind that can no longer judge rightly, a pattern Paul reverses in 12:2, where the renewed mind is able to test and approve God's will (the same verb, dokimazō).

verses.context: A vice list of twenty-one items shows the unfitting conduct of verse 28. Its weight falls on the sins of community life (envy, strife, deceit, gossip, slander, arrogance, disobedience to parents, faithlessness, heartlessness) rather than on sexual sin, so the list reaches every reader. The last four words describe people who cannot keep faith with or show mercy to anyone.
verses.grammar: Peplērōmenous is a perfect passive participle, ‘having been filled’, describing a settled condition that results from God's handing over. Paul groups the list by sound as well as sense: phthonou phonou, ‘envy, murder’, differ by one letter, and verse 31 opens with four words beginning with the negative prefix a-: asynetous, asynthetous, astorgous, aneleēmonas, ‘senseless, faithless, heartless, merciless’, where the first two also rhyme. Theostygeis can be active, ‘God-haters’ (most versions), or passive, ‘hateful to God’, the older Greek sense; in a list of active vices, the active fits better. Epheuretas kakōn, ‘inventors of evils’, describes people creative in wrongdoing.
verses.history: Lists of vices were a standard form in both Greek moral philosophy and Jewish teaching. The Wisdom of Solomon (14:25-26) follows its critique of idolatry with a similar catalogue, and the Community Rule from Qumran (1QS 4:9-11) lists the vices of those who walk in the spirit of falsehood. Paul's own letters contain several (1 Corinthians 6:9-10, Galatians 5:19-21, 2 Timothy 3:2-4).
verses.text: The Textus Receptus adds two words from the Byzantine manuscripts: ‘fornication’ (porneia) in verse 29 and ‘implacable’ (aspondous) in verse 31, both visible in the King James Version. The earliest manuscripts lack them, and modern editions treat them as scribal additions, the second probably borrowed from the similar list in 2 Timothy 3:3.

theology.note: Sin fractures relationships at every level: with God (God-haters), with family (disobedient to parents), and with neighbors (gossips, merciless). The list shows sin as a social condition, not only an individual failing.

verses.context: The indictment ends with its most damning point: people know God's just verdict that such things deserve death, yet they not only do them but approve of those who do. The next verse (2:1) turns on this knowledge: the one who judges others knows the verdict too.
verses.grammar: Hoitines, ‘people who’, again gives a reason. Dikaiōma, ‘righteous decree’ or ‘just requirement’, is a legal term; Paul uses it in 2:26 and 8:4 of the law's requirement. Epignontes, an aorist participle, is concessive, ‘although they know’. The climax rests on the contrast between poiousin, ‘they do’, and syneudokousin, ‘they approve’: to endorse evil in others is presented as worse than committing it, because it makes wrongdoing a shared standard rather than a private failure.

theology.note: Even without the written law, people know that God's just order condemns what they do. This is the knowledge Paul will call the law written on the heart (2:15), and it leaves every person answerable to God.

Death is the just desert of sin, a theme Paul will state plainly in 6:23. The verdict is known before it is pronounced, which makes the coming judgment a confirmation of what conscience already testified.
